S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
examples: Focuses at first during class or meetings but soon becomes distracted or spaces out.
Re-reads the same paragraph in a book multiple times but the content does not register.
Loses focus while watching movies or TV and misses the plot.
Unable to maintain attention until the end of a long meeting or lecture, often drifting off or becoming drowsy.

S003.name: Listening_Difficulty
S003.description: Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
examples: Appears not to be listening, looking elsewhere or spacing out during conversation.
Immediately asks to repeat what was just said or instructed.
Does not respond when name is called or answers only after a long delay.
Misses the content of the conversation, giving unrelated answers or out-of-context reactions.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
examples: Starts homework or projects but fails to complete them, submitting unfinished work or missing deadlines.
When given multi-step instructions, follows only the first few steps and forgets the rest.
Starts cleaning or organizing but switches to another task midway, failing to finish.
Leaves almost completed work reports or paperwork unfinished, neglecting the final steps.

S006.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
S006.description: Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort.
examples: Continually procrastinates or is reluctant to start writing long reports or complex homework.
Avoids activities that require long periods of concentration, such as reading books or studying.
Passes off tasks that require complex thinking or planning to others.
Gets annoyed or resists when asked to start a task that requires significant mental effort.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
examples: Frequently loses school supplies or office supplies like pens, erasers, and calculators.
Always searching for glasses, cell phones, wallets, or keys because they do not know where they are.
Loses necessary documents or materials at home or in the office and cannot find them.
Cannot remember where they placed an item they were holding just moments ago.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention such as difficulty sustaining focus, disorganization, distractibility, and forgetfulness, without the prominent hyperactive or impulsive behaviors seen in other ADHD presentations. Symptoms must be developmentally inappropriate, present for at least six months, and cause clinically significant impairment in academic, occupational, or social functioning, with onset in childhood even if diagnosis is delayed until adulthood. The course is often chronic, though the way impairment manifests can change across the lifespan as environmental demands shift (e.g., transitions in schooling, job complexity, or caregiving roles). It is distinguished from anxiety and mood disorders by the pervasiveness and early onset of attentional difficulties, and from cognitive disorders by its stability over time and lack of progressive decline.

patient.stressor: Jason formally retired from paid handyman work a little over two years ago, shifting his time into structured volunteering as an arts liaison and planning workshops for seniors. Without the concrete, hands-on jobs and daily routines he had relied on for decades, he began noticing how hard it was to keep track of multi-step plans for gallery walks, lecture series, and his own photography projects, despite carefully written notes and printed maps. As he took on more responsibility coordinating volunteers and communicating with museum staff, he became increasingly frustrated by how often he would start organizing one event and then drift off into reading about art history or rearranging his photo archive, only to realize later that key tasks had been left incomplete. Concerned that his long-standing tendency to "zone out" was becoming more disruptive in this new phase of life, and worried it might signal early cognitive decline, he consulted his primary care physician, who then referred him for a psychiatric assessment to clarify whether his persistent difficulties fit an inattentive ADHD pattern rather than a neurocognitive disorder.
patient.chief_complaint: “Since I stopped working full-time, I keep starting projects for the museum and then just never finishing them, even when I really want to.”

S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
S002.manifestation: When I sit in on those long planning meetings at the museum, I’ll be following along for the first few minutes and then my mind just drifts off to thinking about lighting for a photo I want to take, and by the time I snap back I’ve missed a chunk of what they were talking about.

S003.name: Listening_Difficulty
S003.description: Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
S003.manifestation: My wife and the folks at the gallery will tell me something, like what time we’re meeting or which room we’re using, and I’ll be looking right at them but it’s like the words don’t land, because five minutes later I have to ask them to repeat it.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
S004.manifestation: I’ll start setting up a workshop—send a couple of emails, pull out the flyers, maybe start a sign‑up sheet—and then I get sidetracked sorting old photos or reading about a new exhibit, and a week later I realize I never finished confirming the room or calling the last few people on the list.

S006.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
S006.description: Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort.
S006.manifestation: If I know a task is going to mean sitting still and really concentrating, like writing out a detailed schedule for the month or reading through a stack of museum emails, I keep putting it off and finding little chores to do instead, even though I know it’ll hang over my head until I finally force myself to do it.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
S007.manifestation: I’m always misplacing the things I need for this volunteer work—my reading glasses, the little notebook with all my dates, even the folder with the workshop forms—and I end up walking from room to room retracing my steps because I set them down somewhere without noticing.

add_requirements.Onset prior to age 12 years: Even back in elementary school, teachers were always telling my parents that I was bright but constantly daydreaming, losing track of instructions, and forgetting to hand in homework I’d actually done.
add_requirements.functional_impairment: Since retiring, my spacing out and losing track of details has meant I’ve double-booked rooms, missed email deadlines, and had to apologize to museum staff and other volunteers when events weren’t fully organized, which makes me feel unreliable and hesitant to take on new responsibilities.
add_requirements.duration: These problems have really come to a head over the last couple of years since I retired and started volunteering at the museum, when the planning and organizing demands picked up and I could no longer just rely on my old routines.
